title: What adab means
hookLine: adab is courtesy toward Allah, people and things

lines: A HAND ALL OVER THE DISH.
cards: A boy is eating at the Prophet's table, and his hand is wandering all over the shared dish, reaching here, reaching there.

Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the moment, told by the boy himself, Umar ibn Abi Salamah, who was being raised in the Prophet's household. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, doesn't scold him or send him away.
He gives him three short instructions. And with them, a new part of the path begins: manners, and the word that holds them. Today: adab.

teach.h: SAY THE NAME, RIGHT HAND, NEAR SIDE.
teach.b: Here's what he told the boy: young man, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you. Three instructions, reaching in three directions.
Saying Allah's name is courtesy toward Allah. Eating from what's in front of you, not reaching across everyone's side, is courtesy toward the people at the table.
And the right hand is a habit for the body itself, the way the meal is held.
Adab is the word for that whole web: manners, courtesy, the right way to be with Allah, with people, and with things. Second, why it isn't small.
The Qur'an praises the Prophet's character in one line, met back on day six hundred forty-one, in Pickthall's words: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature."
Manners aren't decoration on top of faith; they're how character shows up at a table. Third, courtesy reaches past people.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim says Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, and gives a hard example: when you slaughter, sharpen the blade and spare the animal. Things and creatures are owed courtesy too.
And last, the boy. In al-Bukhari's report, he says that was how he ate from then on. Not a rule memorized.
A habit given gently, at the right moment, that stayed.

how: Muslims learn adab, the manners of daily life, from the Prophet's example: saying bismillah before eating, eating with the right hand and from what is nearest, greeting, and treating people, animals and things with care.

strict rules of etiquette for formal dinners

games.q: you're the boy at the Prophet's table, your hand wandering all over the shared dish. what does he tell you?
o: leave the table until you can behave.
say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, eat from what's in front of you.

games.why: three gentle instructions, no scolding. in al-Bukhari's report, the boy says that became how he ate from then on.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing you'll do today and picture doing it with adab, slowly, with care.

A meal begun with the name of Allah, if that's yours to say, eaten from your own side; a door held and closed gently; a borrowed book put back the way you found it; a message answered with a greeting first.
If you pray, you can ask for good manners.

wordCard.voice: Adab. Courtesy and good manners toward Allah, people and things; the right way to do an ordinary thing. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: manners, courtesy, the right way of doing a thing.
